control_ladder.note_beginner: When a clump goes streaky and papery, cut it right down to the base and carry the trimmings out of the garden. The insects leave with the blades you take off, and chives push up fresh green leaves that start clean.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A hard shear to the base is the reset for a marked clump: it carries the resident population out with the foliage and forces clean regrowth. Remove what you cut rather than leaving it at the edge of the bed, and treat it as the first move in a heavy year rather than the last.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A jet from the hose knocks thrips loose while numbers are still low. Point it down into the crease where the blades overlap, because they feed tucked in there rather than out on the open leaf. Do it in the morning so the foliage has the day to dry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Thrips sit down in the leaf axils, the folds where one blade wraps the next, so aim the jet into those folds rather than across the open blade. Use it as the physical knock-down under light pressure, in the morning so leaf wetness does not carry into the evening.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lacewings and minute pirate bugs, two small helpful insects that feed on thrips, do steady work on a chive clump. Leave them room by holding off on broad insect sprays, which take them out along with the pest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserving the resident predators, minute pirate bugs and lacewings among them, is the standing control on a crop where the feeding damage is usually cosmetic. A broad-spectrum material costs more here than the streaking does, since it removes the enemies holding the population flat.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If streaking keeps spreading after the water and the shear, insecticidal soap on the leaves is the next step. It works only where it lands, so wet the folds the thrips are sitting in. Give harvested blades a rinse before they go in the kitchen.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is a contact material and the leaf axils are the hard part of the coverage, so a pass that misses the folds misses much of the population. It can burn foliage above 90°F or on a drought-stressed clump, which is the same hot, dry weather thrips build in, so water first and spray in the cool part of the day. Rinse harvested leaves.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spinosad is a stronger organic spray, worth considering only in a bad year that has run past soap. It is hard on bees while it is fresh, so spray at dusk and keep it off a clump that is in flower. Rinse the leaves before you use them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad is the step past soap for a season when thrips pressure warrants it, and it comes after the shear, the water pass and the conserved predators rather than instead of them. It is hard on bees while wet and for roughly a day after, so the pass goes on at dusk, on a clump that is out of bloom, and the leaves are rinsed before use.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put a new chive planting on ground that has not just carried alliums, the onion family that chives, onions, garlic and leeks belong to. Starting away from a spot that was mined last season cuts what carries over into the new plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Siting a new planting away from allium ground that was mined recently lowers what carries over into it, and keeping it apart from other allium beds under pressure does the same for what arrives from outside. The fly is specific to the onion family and works two flights a year, spring and fall.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Any blade carrying a wavy pale tunnel, or the line of white dots punched down it, should come off the plant and go out with the trash rather than onto the ground beside the bed. The maggots, and the brown seed-shaped pupae that are the resting stage between maggot and adult, sit inside that tissue at the leaf bases. Clear plant debris off the bed too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mined foliage carries the larvae, and the puparia lodge in the leaf sheaths, so stripping it removes the developing generation rather than tidying the clump. Sanitize crop residue on the same pass, and destroy what you take off. Larval wounds also open the way for secondary bacterial and fungal rots, which is a second reason not to leave mined leaves standing.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Floating row cover is a light fabric you lay over the planting; sun and rain pass through and the fly cannot. It must go on before each flight: in early spring ahead of the first flies, and again before September for the fall flight, since a cover laid after eggs are in the leaves shuts nothing out. Tuck the edges in. Do not lay it over a bed that grew onion-family plants last year, or you seal emerging flies in with the chives.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Phytomyza gymnostoma has two flights, roughly March into May and September into October, and the cover only works if it is up ahead of each one; adults lay into leaves they can reach, so exclusion laid after the rows of white punctures appear is late. Seal the edges. Put it on ground that carried no alliums last season; a cover over last year's mined bed traps the emerging flies under it with the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where the flies are heavy, spinosad is a stronger organic spray that can help. Bees are harmed by it while it is fresh, so spray at dusk and skip any planting that is in flower.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad is the stronger organic material for a planting where leafminer pressure runs high, and it follows exclusion and the removal of mined foliage rather than standing in for either. Bees are at risk while it is wet and for roughly a day after, so apply at dusk and only to a planting that is not in bloom.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give chives a spot away from wherever onions, garlic, leeks or chives grew last year, and do not set a new clump back into that ground. The fly passes the winter as pupae, its resting stage, in the soil around last year's onion-family plants, and in spring the new flies climb out of that same ground, so a bed across the garden keeps the clump out of their way.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotate off last season's allium ground and keep the new planting at a distance from it, not merely out of it. Delia antiqua overwinters as pupae in the soil around the previous year's alliums and the first spring generation emerges from that soil, so proximity to an old allium bed is what exposes a new clump. With no home-garden insecticide for larvae in the crown, siting carries much of the weight.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear old bulbs, culls (the small or damaged plants you pulled and did not use) and any onion-family plants that came up on their own out of the bed and out of the garden, because rotting onion material is what draws the fly in to lay. If a clump is wilting with maggots in its base, dig it up roots and all and get rid of it. In spring, keep fresh manure out of the bed for the same reason.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sanitation works on the attractant and on the overwintering stage at once. Culls, volunteer alliums and rotting organic matter, fresh manure and green manure included, draw egg-laying, so clear them and hold manure out of the bed in spring; plants lifted in fall with their roots carry the pupae out of the ground with them. Rogue infested plants with the root ball and destroy them, since no home-garden insecticide reaches larvae already in the crown.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put floating row cover on the day the chives go in, before the spring flies are out. It is a light fabric that lets sun and water through, and with the edges buried the fly cannot reach the base of a plant, which is where it lays. Use it only on ground that did not grow onions, garlic, leeks or chives last year: a bed that carried them last season has flies waiting in its soil, and a cover seals them in with the crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Timing and seal decide this one. Delia antiqua lays at the base of the plant, so the fabric goes on from planting, sealed at the edges, ahead of the spring flight; put on after the first generation has laid, it protects little. Rotation is its precondition: the pupae sit in the soil around last season's alliums, so a bed that carried alliums last year has the next generation under the fabric from the start, and sealing it traps them with the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give clumps room, and split crowded ones, so air moves through the leaves. This disease runs where damp foliage stays damp, and a stand that dries quickly is a poorer place for it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Dividing crowded clumps and spacing them shortens the leaf wetness this oomycete depends on. It favors cool, humid weather, below about 75°F, and a dense stand holds exactly those conditions, so the layout decision is made before the weather arrives rather than in response to it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Site chives where water drains away and the sun reaches them. Soggy, shaded ground holds the dampness this disease needs, and a crowded planting on wet ground is where it spreads fastest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Poorly drained ground holds the moisture that sustains the pathogen, so drainage and exposure are worth settling before a clump goes in. On heavy or low-lying ground, correct that first rather than leaning on spacing and watering to make up for it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Deliver the water down at the soil line and keep it off the foliage. This disease travels on the wind, so you cannot keep it from arriving, but it needs wet leaves to take hold, and watering low keeps the blades dry for as long as the weather lets you.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Basal irrigation holds leaf wetness to what the weather imposes. The pathogen arrives on the wind and needs a long wet period on the blade to infect, so this is the practice half of the defense that spacing sets at planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Take off affected leaves as you notice them, and if a clump is badly hit, cut it to the base so it regrows once the weather turns drier. Get the cuttings out of the garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Strip infected foliage, and shear a heavily affected clump so the regrowth comes on under drier conditions. Once it is established the home garden has no reliable cure, which is what puts the weight on removing tissue and on spacing, drainage and dry foliage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Thin out a crowded planting and split big clumps so air can move between the blades. Rust shows up most in wet seasons and in crowded stands where the leaves stay damp, so the room you give them at planting is the first thing that works against it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Puccinia rust is favored by moisture and by a dense stand, and the two arrive together in a clump that has closed up. Divide to open it, and set spacing so the blades dry quickly after rain, since the urediniospores travel on air and need humid weather to take; the layout cannot stop arrival, only shorten the wet period they land in.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hold back on nitrogen fertilizer. Rust is worse on over-fed plants, because the lush growth heavy feeding pushes is what the fungus does best on, and a clump fed hard grows dense again, closing up the airflow you opened. Feed chives lightly, and keep nitrogen moderate rather than heavy.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen is one of the three conditions this rust is tied to, alongside moisture and crowding, and it feeds the other two: lush growth is the tissue the fungus favors, and a heavily fed clump closes back up and holds its leaves wet longer. Keep nitrogen moderate from the start of the season rather than cutting it once pustules show, since by then the growth is already there.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put the hose at the base of the clump instead of sprinkling over it. Watering from above leaves the blades wet, and a wet leaf in humid weather is where the orange spots get started, so keep the foliage as dry as the weather allows.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Irrigate at the soil line. The urediniospores arrive on the wind, so this does nothing to stop them landing; what it changes is how long the blade stays wet once they have, and humid, wet foliage is the condition they need. Overhead watering adds hours of wetness the weather did not impose, and that is the part of the wet period the gardener controls.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut off leaves with orange spots and throw them away, or, if the rust is all through the clump, shear the whole thing to the base so it comes back clean. Do it as soon as you see the spots, before they spread. At the end of the season, clear the dead leaves and trimmings out of the bed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A hard cut to the base removes the pustules with the foliage and the clump regrows clean; for a light case, taking off the spotted blades early, before it spreads and before heavy infection yellows the leaves, is the move. Get the cut material out of the bed rather than dropping it beside the clump, and clear the debris at season's end. Fungicides are rarely warranted on a home planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with clean plants from a source you trust, and do not bring in soil from a garden that has had this disease. An affected spot cannot be cured, so what you settle before planting counts for far more than anything you do afterward.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Clean, sclerotia-free stock is settled at purchase, and it carries more weight on this disease than on most because an infested site has no rescue. Sclerotia are the fungus's resting bodies, and a dirty division or a scoop of imported soil is how they arrive in a clean bed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a spot has had white rot, keep chives, onions and garlic out of it and put new onion-family plants on fresh ground. What the fungus leaves in the soil is a scatter of hard black survival bodies the size of poppy seeds, and they wait there for many years until another allium arrives.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Long rotation is the standing management, and its length comes from the sclerotia, which persist for many years and can leave a site unusable for alliums for a decade or more. Treat infested ground as quarantined from the onion family rather than as a bed on a rotation clock.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Dig up a plant with white rot together with the soil around its roots, and get rid of both; the plant will not recover, and the soil now carries the fungus. Wash the soil off your tools before you work in another bed, and do not move that dirt, or plants from it, anywhere else in the garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rogue out infected plants with the surrounding soil: the sclerotia form in abundance at the base alongside the white mycelium, and they move on soil, on tools and on planting material. Sanitize tools after working the infested spot and do not carry divisions or soil out of it; on this disease sanitation is containment, keeping a decade-long problem to the bed that has it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Divide crowded clumps and give each one room, so air moves through the leaves and they dry after rain or watering. This blight only gets going when the leaves stay wet for most of a day in cool weather, and a crowded, still planting is exactly where they stay wet that long.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Botrytis squamosa infects only where leaf wetness lasts 20 hours or more, and a dense chive stand with poor air circulation is what supplies that duration; the spores are airborne, so arrival is not the variable, drying time is. Divide and space so the canopy dries well inside the 20-hour window after rain or irrigation, and keep dividing as the clumps close up, since spacing set at planting drifts on a perennial.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, and do it at a time of day that lets the blades dry off before night. The spots form only after the leaves have been wet for most of a day, so watering that wets the foliage in the evening hands the fungus the long wet stretch it needs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Irrigate at the soil line and time it so the foliage is dry before night, since the infection threshold is 20 or more hours of leaf wetness and an evening overhead watering carries the wet period straight through the night. The spores are airborne, so watering low does not keep them off the leaves; what it buys is a shorter wet period, which on a perennial cut and regrown all season is the one variable the gardener sets.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the leaves are spotting, cut the clump back hard and carry the cut leaves out of the bed rather than leaving them where they fall, so the new growth comes up clean. At the end of the season, clear away the dead foliage and any plants you pulled, because the fungus spends the winter in old chive leaves and starts from there next year.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Shear the clump and remove the cut foliage instead of leaving it in the bed: sclerotia form on infected leaves, and they are the overwintering stage, persisting in the soil for months to years. Clear dead foliage, culls and debris at the end of the season for the same reason. Fungicides are seldom warranted on a home chive planting, so removal is the treatment, not a step before one.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a bed has carried chives, onions, garlic or leeks with this blight, keep new plantings off it for three years. The fungus survives in the old leaves and debris left in that soil, so a fresh spot starts a new clump away from what is waiting there.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Keep new plantings off ground that carried diseased alliums for three years. The sclerotia that overwinter on infected leaves, culls and debris persist in the soil for months to years, so the rotation length is set by their survival rather than by the crop's cycle, and it applies to where a new or divided clump is set.
